analysis.one_liner: Fast-tracks federal approval of the Keystone XL pipeline by stripping the President's permit authority.
analysis.headline: With 103 Republican cosponsors, the bill cleared committee on a 33-20 vote and was placed on the House calendar on December 17, 2012 — but the House never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have handed the developer of the Keystone XL oil pipeline a federal construction permit within 30 days, with no added conditions, and would have declared that no presidential permit — normally required for a pipeline crossing an international border — is needed at all. If the energy regulator didn't act within 30 days, the permit would count as approved automatically. The pipeline could start construction outside Nebraska even while the disputed Nebraska route was still being worked out.
analysis.who_benefits: The pipeline's developer, TransCanada, and the Canadian oil sands producers whose crude it would carry, get what normal permitting had denied them: a guaranteed federal permit on a 30-day clock, without added conditions, and without the President able to say no. Gulf Coast refineries would gain a new source of heavy crude. Construction companies and pipeline workers would gain jobs during the build-out — the argument supporters most often made on behalf of the public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The pipeline developer and oil producers

how_it_helps.text: FERC would be required to issue a permit for the pipeline 'without additional conditions' within 30 days of an application, implementing it according to the existing environmental impact statement.
If FERC had not acted within 30 days, the permit would be deemed issued automatically — the developer would not need a favorable decision at all.
The bill declares that no presidential permit shall be required, overriding the executive orders that had governed cross-border pipelines, which removes the President's authority to deny the project.
While a revised Nebraska route was still under review, the permit holder could 'commence or continue' construction of every portion of the pipeline outside Nebraska.

analysis.who_pays: The public would give up the normal checks on a cross-border pipeline: the President's permit authority would be eliminated, the regulator would be barred from adding conditions, and a formal Record of Decision under environmental review law would not be required [S3, S4]. The people along the route — particularly in Nebraska, where the line crosses sensitive groundwater — would bear the spill and construction risk with the fastest possible review clock, and any promise of consumer energy benefit rests on oil that is priced in a global market.

drawbacks.text: The permit must be issued 'without additional conditions' and FERC is not required to prepare a Record of Decision — meaning the approval would come with less environmental paperwork and less regulatory leverage than the ordinary process provides.
The deemed-approval provisions mean inaction on a 30-day clock counts as a yes, so the developer gets a permit even if the regulator never makes a decision.
Construction could begin outside Nebraska before the contested Nebraska route was resolved, committing the project to the ground while the hardest question was still open.
Removing the presidential permit requirement for a pipeline crossing an international border sets aside the standard process entirely for this one project.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow overwhelmingly to a single developer and the oil producers it serves; whatever the public gets — construction jobs, oil supply — comes bundled with the removal of the President's permit authority, a no-conditions permit on a 30-day clock, and an expedited Nebraska review with an automatic-approval backstop. The bill is drafted so the project cannot be slowed or conditioned by any federal regulator, which is the opposite of accountability.

outcome.mechanism: The committee reported the bill and placed it on the House calendar on December 17, 2012, but with two weeks left in the Congress no floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Lee Terry introduced the bill on December 2, 2011, and it was referred to three committees.
The House Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported on a 33-20 recorded vote on February 7, 2012, but did not formally report it until December 17, 2012, as House Report 112-703.

On December 17, 2012, the Transportation and Natural Resources committees were discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 515 — days before the 112th Congress adjourned on January 3, 2013.
The House never took up the bill, so it died on the calendar without a vote in either chamber.
The bill was written as an end-run around President Obama, who had denied the Keystone XL permit in January 2012 — which is why it eliminated the presidential permit requirement entirely.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people and groups who wanted the pipeline to stay subject to presidential approval and full environmental review — they kept the existing process intact, at least for another Congress. TransCanada got no approval through this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of a fast-tracked pipeline permit

for.name: Lee Terry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 103 cosponsors, all Republicans.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported 33-20 in February 2012 and formally reported it amended on December 17, 2012.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote in the two weeks after it was placed on the calendar, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: 20 members of the Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee members who opposed the bill at markup
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported, 33-20.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Had denied the Keystone XL presidential permit in January 2012; the bill was drafted to remove that authority, and the pipeline remained blocked through the end of his first term.

sides.party_line_note: All 103 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee reported the bill on a 33-20 vote; no Democrat is recorded in support.

industries.note: The bill exists to give one pipeline a guaranteed federal permit on a 30-day clock with no added conditions and no presidential check. The developer's gain comes from skipping the normal review that communities along the route would otherwise rely on.
A built Keystone XL would give landlocked Canadian heavy crude a route to Gulf Coast markets. The faster the permit, the sooner the producers' product can flow.
Refineries configured for heavy crude would gain a new feedstock source, which supporters argued lowers input costs — though refined products sell into a global market.
Construction firms and pipeline trades would gain work on the build-out, including the provision allowing construction outside Nebraska to start immediately while the route dispute was pending.
